How do I find all of the apt-get names of all of the dependencies of a program I got from a git repo?
For .deb packages, dpkg -I file.deb. For others try apt-cache depends PackageName

If you are talking about finding the dependencies for source code you will need to review the readme or install document provided in the source code. If the dependencies are not listed in either of those documents or those docs dont exist you will need to try to compile the code and see what libraries it complains about not having. Then you should be able to take the library name and google it to find what package provides it. Make sure you install the development packages for any dependency.
I'm on my phone right now, but it was asking for libcurl 7.44 or something, which didn't even seem to exist.

Use "apt-cache search curl". You should find a curl-devel package or curl-dev something like that. This is pretty standard for compiling packages from source. The library may resemble the package name, but it might not. So search the web for library-name package ubuntu (or whatever your distro is) if you cant find a package that matches the library in question.

You should install the dev or devel package in addition to the main curl package because most times when compiling source code you need the development package for the library's headers.

*edit luckyguy is correct about the dual packaging of libcurl. It looks like my ubuntu server boxes have the gnutls version by default. To see if you have libcurl installed already use dpkg and grep like so: "dpkg --list | grep curl"

If you have one installed go ahead and install the corresponding -dev package.

libcurl is packaged two different ways depending on the encryption library that's staticly linked to it. libcurl-gnutls, and libcurl-openssl I think. This is a problem that shows it's head every now and again. This is where I've found graphical systems to be useful. Synaptic can usually help you. Back when I needed to do that sort of thing on servers more than I do now I would use usually ubuntu server and debian desktop and I could always research what I need on the desktop and know what to type on the server.

Then you should be able to take the library name and google it to find what package provides it.

The apt-file search foo utility on Debian derivatives and yum provides foo utility on RedHat derivatives are very handy for going down that rabbit hole.

A few suggestions here, auto-apt could be what you're looking for but from my past experience many years ago it's a lot more of a hassle (it usually works though) than finding the proper dependency list on a README, BUILD or INSTALL file or website - or even just trying apt-get build-dep first http://www.howtogeek.com/106526/how-to-resolve-dependencies-while-compiling-software-on-ubuntu/
